HL7 v2 and FHIR: Orders, Results, ADT, and the Messages Imaging Runs On

Unit 1: Imaging Informatics Foundations. Lesson 3 of 65 in CIIP Academy.

Orders from the EMR stop appearing in the RIS at 06:40. Nothing is down. This is the kind of problem that HL7 knowledge solves in minutes.

What an HL7 v2 message is

A message is a set of segments, one per line. Each segment is a row of fields separated by pipe characters. The first segment, MSH, names the sender, the receiver, the message type, and a control ID. PID identifies the patient, PV1 describes the visit, ORC is the common order, OBR is the observation request (the ordered procedure), and OBX carries a line of result.

The messages imaging uses

  • ADT carries registration, updates, and merges to the RIS and PACS.
  • ORM or OMI carries new, changed, or cancelled orders.
  • ORU carries the report text and status back to the EMR.
  • SIU carries scheduling.
  • MDM carries documents and their status.

Delivery and acknowledgment

Messages travel over TCP wrapped by MLLP. The receiver answers with an ACK. An interface engine receives, routes, maps, and queues messages. A stalled queue is the first place to look when orders stop.

FHIR

FHIR models health data as small resources reached by plain web calls: Patient, ServiceRequest (the order), ImagingStudy, and DiagnosticReport. Many sites run HL7 v2 inside and FHIR at the edges, such as for portals and apps.

Where HL7 meets DICOM

The two worlds meet in the accession number (the ordered exam) and the patient ID with its issuer. If they differ, the study cannot match its order.

Exam tip: orders are ORM or OMI, results are ORU, patient events and merges are ADT. An order that never arrives means check the interface engine queue first.
Remember
HL7 v2 messages are pipe-delimited segments sent through an interface engine, and the accession number and patient ID are the keys that tie them to the DICOM images.
Deeper explanation

HL7 v2 and FHIR: Orders, Results, ADT, and the Messages Imaging Runs On, explained slowly

An order and its result, line by line

Below are an order from the EMR to the RIS and the result coming back. Read them segment by segment.

MSH|^~\&|EMR|MAINHOSP|RIS|MAINHOSP|20261123081500||ORM^O01|MSG00045|P|2.3
PID|1||MR123456^^^MAINHOSP^MR||DOE^JANE||19700412|F
PV1|1|O|XRAY^^^MAINHOSP
ORC|NW|ORD7781
OBR|1|ORD7781|ACC20261123001|CXR2^Chest 2 views

MSH|^~\&|RPT|MAINHOSP|EMR|MAINHOSP|20261123103000||ORU^R01|MSG00112|P|2.3
PID|1||MR123456^^^MAINHOSP^MR||DOE^JANE||19700412|F
ORC|RE|ORD7781
OBR|1|ORD7781|ACC20261123001|CXR2^Chest 2 views
OBX|1|TX|RPT^Report||No acute findings||||||F

What each part means

  • The MSH segment gives sender, receiver, time, message type (an order, then a result), and a control ID the ACK will quote.
  • PID field 3 holds the identifier list: here MR123456 issued by MAINHOSP. Field 5 holds the name, family name first, with a caret between components.
  • ORC says what to do with the order: NW is a new order, RE is an observation or result.
  • OBR names the placer order number (ORD7781, assigned by the EMR) and the filler order number (the accession, assigned by the RIS), and the procedure.
  • OBX carries one line of result in field 5. The last populated field, F, is the result status: final.

Worked diagnosis

Radiology says the result never appears in the chart. You find the result message in the engine log with a negative acknowledgment and the error that the order ORD7781 is unknown. The cause: the order was changed, which created a new placer number, but the reporting system still used the old one. The fix is in the order message handling, not in the chart.

Acknowledgment values

An accepted message is answered with an acknowledgment code AA, an application error with AE, a rejection with AR. An interface engine resends or holds a message that gets an error and raises an alert for anything it cannot deliver. Leaving the queue to grow silently is the failure to avoid. Ask for the queue depth and the oldest message age every morning, because those two numbers show a stall long before a clinician calls.
